title: Coping with Pressure at Work
author: Kate
summary: Writing to leaders who feel squeezed between execution, innovation, accountability and empathy, the author of The Good Busy shares how she copes with pressure. She opens with a teenage tennis tournament where she went from undefeated to losing 6-0, 6-0 in a day, and uses it to argue that you control only your own mind, and even that is hard under emotional pressure. Watching tennis players glance at their box between points leads her to the claim that no one sustains the mental game alone. She lists her own team: managers who allowed honesty, a therapist, an executive coach, yoga teachers, close friends, her sister and her dog. She notes that digital life and AI can deepen isolation among leaders. Her practical play of the week is to ask who is on your team, or who you can bring onto it.
points: Leaders often hold others to impossible standards and so hold themselves to the same ones, which produces the fatigue behind questions about balancing pressure and empathy.
Calm on the outside does not mean calm inside, and even the best performers describe an inner storm they have to manage.
A personal support team can include managers, therapists, coaches, friends and family, each doing a different job, and no one of them has to do it all.
Coaches differ from therapists by focusing on where you are headed, which helps because the destination keeps moving.
The weekly practice is to name who is on your team, or to recruit one doubles partner, rather than carry pressure alone.
quotes: We hold others to impossible standards. And because of it, we hold ourselves to impossible standards too.

Back in my corporate days, the unspoken expectation was to deliver everything, without room for mistake (or emotion.) And also to be the endlessly patient, available, understanding, and protective manager for my team.
No person can sustain that mental game alone. It’s too intense.
I understood that we can’t expect empathy, when we don’t let people see us from the inside.
Coaches are different from therapists. They rarely dig into the past. They help you see where you’re headed and how to get there, especially because that destination keeps moving.
Many leaders I work with feel alone. One of the most common messages I get after my free workshop is “It was really good to know I’m not alone.
This week, ask yourself who is on your team. Or who can you bring onto your team.
